name: Mauritania
summary: A desert country between the Arab world and West Africa, independent from France in 1960; slavery was abolished only in 1981.

knownFor.label: Iron ore train
knownFor.note: One of the longest trains in the world.

terrain.value: Mostly Sahara desert, sand dunes and rocky plateaus such as the Adrar; the Senegal River valley in the south is the main farmland.

climate.value: Hot desert over most of the country with very little rain; the south has a short rainy season, and the coast is cooled by sea breezes.

resources.value: Iron ore from Zouérat, rich fishing grounds off the coast, gold and copper, and offshore gas fields.

disasters.value: Droughts and locust swarms; the Sahel droughts of the 1970s and 1980s killed herds and pushed nomads into towns.

population.value: 5,461,319 in a 2026 estimate; about 4.6 million in 2021 and 0.7 million in 1950.

urbanisation.value: Now mostly urban: Nouakchott, built as the capital from 1958, has over a million people; Nouadhibou is the second city.

disease.value: Malaria in the south and child malnutrition in drought years; health services are concentrated in Nouakchott.

migration.value: Droughts drove many nomads into towns; in 1989 tens of thousands of Black Mauritanians were expelled to Senegal and Mali.

economicBase.value: Mainly agriculture and fishing; iron ore is almost 50% of exports and oil was discovered in 2001.

tradeRoutes.value: A railway of about 700 km carries iron ore from Zouérat to the port of Nouadhibou; Nouakchott is the main port for imports.

moneyAndTax.value: The ouguiya, introduced in 1973 when Mauritania left the CFA franc zone; a new ouguiya replaced it in 2018.

inequality.value: Large gaps between the capital and rural areas.

governmentType.value: A unitary semi-presidential Islamic republic with a directly elected president; independence on 28 November 1960.

keyRulers.value: Moktar Ould Daddah made it a one-party state in 1964 and was ousted in a coup on 10 July 1978; later rulers came to power by coups (1978, 2005, 2008) and elections. Later and present leaders are not named here.
keyRulers.source: Wikipedia: Mauritania (checked 13 Nov 2026); Britannica: Mauritania history (checked 15 Nov 2026) (the first president was deposed in a military coup in July 1978; the page does not give 10 July or the 1964 one-party constitution)

institutions.value: A president, a single-chamber National Assembly (the Senate was abolished in 2017) and courts using Islamic and civil law.

stability.value: Coups: Daddah ousted on 10 July 1978; Taya deposed Haidallah in December 1984; 6 August 2008.

eliteConflict.value: Competition between political parties and leaders.

armyAndTech.value: A small army with desert and camel units; it fought in Western Sahara until 1979 and later against armed groups in the Sahel.
armyAndTech.source: Wikipedia: Mauritania; Wikipedia: Western Sahara (checked 18 Nov 2026)

majorWars.value: The Western Sahara War: Mauritania took the southern third of Western Sahara in 1976 and withdrew in 1979 after military losses to the Polisario Front.
majorWars.source: Wikipedia: Mauritania (checked 13 Nov 2026); Britannica: Mauritania history (checked 15 Nov 2026); Wikipedia: Western Sahara (checked 18 Nov 2026)

territoryChange.value: Gave up its claim in Western Sahara (1979).

alliancesRivals.value: A member of the Arab League (from 1973) and the African Union; it left ECOWAS in 2000 and had tense relations with Senegal in 1989–91.

inventions.value: No major inventions are associated with the modern state.

scienceEducation.value: Traditional mahadra (Koranic) schools and old manuscript libraries in Chinguetti and Ouadane; the University of Nouakchott opened in 1981.

openness.value: Open to trade and foreign investment, with periods of restriction.

communicationTransport.value: The iron ore train, one of the world’s longest, a coastal highway from Nouakchott to Nouadhibou, and the Rosso ferry to Senegal.

religion.value: Islam is the state religion and almost all inhabitants are Sunni Muslims. Slavery was officially abolished in 1905, 1981 and 2007, and the 2018 Global Slavery Index estimated about 90,000 enslaved people (2.1%).

languageWriting.value: Arabic is official and Hassaniya Arabic is widely spoken; Pulaar, Soninke and Wolof are national languages, and French is used in business.

artsArchitecture.value: Stone desert towns such as Chinguetti, Ouadane, Tichitt and Oualata (UNESCO sites), and the music of griots (iggawen).

socialStructure.value: Moors and Black Africans; descendants of slaves still face discrimination.

sharedIdentity.value: A shared Islamic identity, but tension between an Arab-Berber (Moorish) identity and the identities of Black African groups.

dailyLife.value: Nomad tents and town houses; meals of rice, fish, meat, couscous and camel milk, with sweet green mint tea.

neighbours.value: Western Sahara (mostly under Moroccan control), Algeria, Mali, Senegal.
neighbours.source: Wikipedia: Mauritania; Wikipedia: Western Sahara (checked 18 Nov 2026)

ideasReligions.value: Islamic scholarship and Sufi orders such as the Qadiriyya and Tijaniyya; slavery was abolished in 1981 and made a crime in 2007.

colonisation.value: A French colony (part of French West Africa) until 1960.

riseSignals.value: France organised the territory of Mauritania in 1904 and defeated Adrar in 1912; independence on 28 November 1960.
riseSignals.source: Wikipedia: Mauritania (checked 13 Nov 2026); Britannica: Mauritania history (checked 15 Nov 2026) (independence was declared on 28 November 1960 and French pacification lasted until 1912; the page does not mention 1904 or Adrar)

peakPeriod.value: Too recent to judge; iron ore, fishing and gas have brought growth since the 2000s.

declineSignals.value: None that define the country as a whole.

outcome.value: Still in existence as an independent Islamic republic.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
